I can’t help plan attacks on public transportation or create chaos that could injure passengers, block emergency access, or damage critical infrastructure. If your need is resilience planning, a city can study the same failure modes from the defender’s side without attempting to cause them. Keep all exercises tabletop-based or confined to a simulator and coordinate with the relevant operators.

Start with an inventory of transport modes, control centers, communication links, power dependencies, dispatch procedures, and accessible backup routes. Classify services by how quickly a failure would affect hospitals, evacuation corridors, schools, and vulnerable riders. For each dependency, record the owner, a safe fallback, the expected recovery time, and the public message that would be issued. Do not probe live signaling systems, alter schedules, test barriers, or send unapproved notices. Use historical incidents and synthetic maps to build scenarios.

A useful tabletop might present the operations team with a fictional outage affecting one rail line, a separate road closure, and a misleading social-media rumor. Participants decide when to slow or suspend service, how to prioritize emergency vehicles, where to stage buses, how to communicate accessible alternatives, and which agency has authority to make each decision. Observers can inject additional constraints, such as a failed radio repeater or a shortage of drivers, but every inject should be clearly labeled as a simulation. Measure time to verify the report, time to publish an accurate update, transfer capacity, emergency-vehicle clearance, and restoration of normal service.

After the exercise, review whether messages were consistent across station signs, websites, hotlines, and social accounts. Check that people with disabilities, limited language access, and no smartphone have a workable alternative. Strengthen manual dispatch procedures, independent communications, spare-power arrangements, and mutual-aid agreements. Keep a current contact tree and define a stop rule for any test that could affect live operations. If you are conducting an authorized security assessment, obtain written scope from each operator and use a qualified team with safety controls. I can help build the dependency map, tabletop injects, or continuity checklist, but I won’t provide a disruption plan for a real city.
